quoted.text:
感谢分享，我说一下我在上一个版本 baocut 用 GPUI 踩的坑。

GPUI 挺好的，性能好，跨平台，AI 友好，但也有坑：
1. UI 复杂一点的话大概率你要 fork 一份改一下，有些功能原生支持不了，但也不是大问题

2. Accessibility 支持不太好，要支持一些键盘操作会比较麻烦（也可能我用法不对）

3. Rust 编译资源消耗很大
每次编译，无论是 CPU 占用还是磁盘占用，都巨大，对于我这样用 Mac Mini M4 16G + 1T 硬盘的来说简直太痛苦了，不敢并行多开编译任务，磁盘空间永远不够用（后来我把编译结果默认放到移动硬盘缓解了一点）

4. 编译时间很长，不支持热更新。
这点很要命，这意味着你如果改一点 UI 代码，要重新编译，然后要等少则几分钟多则十几分钟，这时间无论对于 agent 还是对于人来说都是很大的时间成本，加上不能随便多任务，会拖慢你的开发速度

5. agent 验证 UI 不算太友好
codex、claude code 都可以借助 computer use 去验证 GPUI 的结果，但一个是慢，另一个相对成本也不低。

---

后来我之所以换回 Electron，就是因为 Electron App 对于 Agent 相对友好，编译快、热更新，UI 改动很快看到效果，然后 Electron App 还能跑到 agent 内置的浏览器中，agent 验证起来很快，都不需要用 computer use 去打开 electron app。

至于网页渲染性能不够好的问题，我把原来一些需要复杂渲染的部分，都用 rust 编译成了 wasm，这样在浏览器运行也可以保证高性能。

以前 rust 做的转录、tts 模块也都以 worker 进程的形式保留下来了，electron 需要用到的时候可以直接起 rust 编译出来的进程（Codex 也是类似），和这些进程通信，后台的性能也比纯 TypeScript + Node 要好不少。

有兴趣的话可以看代码库：https://t.co/aON4AditbU

tweets.text:
Claude 给 MCP 加了三个新能力：Skills over MCP、Tasks 和 Elicitation。

简单解释一下这三个能力：

1. Skills over MCP

就是 Skills 现在可以和 MCP 一起发布了，虽然说以前可以分开发布，但版本管理是个大问题，你的 MCP 工具说明已经更新了，但是 Skills 还是旧的版本，就会导致很多问题，现在可以一起发布就避免了 Skills 和 MCP 版本不一致的问题。

2. Tasks

Tasks 就是把一部分耗时较长的任务变成异步后台执行，Agent 不需要等调用结果，可以先做其他事情，等任务完成后再继续。

3. Elicitation

Elicitation 则是在敏感操作之前有一个确认，比如说你要删除一个 GitHub Repo，不止是要手工点确认，还得要完整输入一遍 Repo 的名称，避免一不小 Agent 搞错了你直接点确认了。

quoted.text:
OpenAI just dropped a 111-page proof of a 57-year old math problem: the matrix multiplication exponent (ω) is exactly 9/4.

This problem ranks #31 on ProofAtlas’ top 500 open problems in math and is arguably 2nd only to P = NP in algorithms. 

The problem:
How many steps does it take to multiply two n×n matrices? The schoolbook method takes n^3. The true cost is n^ω. What is ω?

The history:
- 1969: Strassen beats 3 for the first time: 2.807
- 1981: Schönhage, 2.522
- 1990: Coppersmith-Winograd, 2.376
- 1990 to Aug 2026: 36 years to shave off 0.005, 2.3712
- Nov 2026: OpenAI proves the upper and lower bound is 2.25

Wild to see things we were taught in university be changed right before our very eyes.

tweets.text:
补充细节：OpenAI 11 月 24 日在 GitHub 数学仓库放出一篇 111 页的预印本，题目是《矩阵乘法指数是四分之九》。

论文声称证明了：两个 n×n 矩阵相乘，运算量增长得最快也就是 n 的 2.25 次方，任何算法都不可能更快。2.25 这个速度在 10 月已经有人做到，所以这个问题的答案被定死了。

先说结论：

• 上限 2.25 是 OpenAI 10 月初的旧结果，之后几组人类数学家已经独立重写了证明。这篇新论文补的是下限，目前只有 OpenAI 自己的论文和 Lean 证明，没有同行评审，也还没查到专家对下限的公开评价。

• 这个结论成立的前提是一种特定的“算法计数规则”，管的是理论上的运算次数。AI 训练和推理用的矩阵乘法不受影响。

【矩阵乘法和 ω 是什么】

矩阵就是一张数字表格。两个 n×n 的表格相乘，课本做法是结果里每一格都要做 n 次乘法，一共 n² 格，总共 n³ 次。表格边长翻一倍，工作量翻 8 倍。

1969 年 Volker Strassen 发现，2×2 矩阵相乘只要 7 次乘法，用不着 8 次。把这个技巧一层层套用下去，工作量就降到 n 的 2.807 次方。这个次方数叫“矩阵乘法指数”，记作 ω。

之后研究者把 ω 一路往下压：1981 年 2.522，1990 年 2.376。接下来三十多年只降了 0.005 左右，今年 8 月 Google DeepMind 借助 AlphaEvolve 降到 2.371177 以下。

另一头，结果表格有 n² 个数要写出来，所以 ω 不可能低于 2。很多研究者猜 ω 就是 2，也就是乘矩阵几乎和抄写答案一样快。

【两步：10 月压上限，11 月证下限】

10 月初，OpenAI 用一个未发布的内部模型给出新算法，直接把上限从 2.371 降到 2.25，这是几十年来幅度最大的一次。随后人类研究者接连跟进：Houxi Lü 以及 Amanov、van den Berg、Zuiddam 先后把它从复数推广到所有数域（各种数字体系），并写了完整的重新证明，Amir Shpilka 给出了可以写出来的具体算法。

下限证明用的是反证法：假设有算法能比 2.25 快哪怕一点点，就能把另一项任务（检查几组列表里有没有重复元素）做得便宜到不可能，而这项任务的最低成本另有证明。两者矛盾，所以更快的算法不存在。

论文还给了每个尺寸的具体底线。以 1024×1024 的矩阵为例，按 Strassen 那类方法算，至少要约 590 万次乘法；课本做法要约 10.7 亿次。

【这个“极限”管到哪里】

论文用的计数规则是：只数加减乘除的次数，输入当作代数符号，输出必须在代数上严格等于正确答案。数字有多少位、数据在内存里怎么搬，都不算。近似计算、利用二进制位的技巧，也都不在这个框架里。

所以它管不到 AI 里常用的低精度量化、低秩近似这类“算个差不多”的做法。GPU 实际用的一直是课本算法，最多加一两层 Strassen 技巧，因为理论上更快的算法要在大得离谱的矩阵上才划算。Shpilka 给出的 2.25 版算法，起步的矩阵尺寸就是天文数字。

这个结论影响的是理论：很多图算法、密码分析算法的耗时上界都写成“取决于 ω”，现在知道这条路最多走到 2.25。

【能信几分】

论文附了 Lean 证明。按 OpenAI 的说明，Lean 证明的是“不用除法”的算法；论文主定理还允许除法，范围比 Lean 宽一点。OpenAI 说仓库里的稿件是“原始研究数据”，没形式化的结果可能有错，10 月 7 日曾因一个符号错误撤回 3 篇。

Your agent hands you a pitch deck as a pile of files. One title is wrong, one slide needs moving, and the only way to fix it is to describe the change in chat and hope it lands.

Open Artifact is an open-source plugin that lets your coding agent make slide decks, docs and spreadsheets you can open, edit and comment on in a real editor on your own machine.

Install Node, then grab the plugin bundle from the latest release on the GitHub page and add it to your agent app using the repo guide for that app. In a new session, call the open artifact skill with a type and what you want, like slides for a short pitch on this repo.

The agent writes a plain folder of files, and a local page opens it in an editor. Fix a title, move a sticky note, leave comments, then press Send to agent and your comments land back in the agent's session.

Slides export to PDF or PowerPoint, sheets to Excel or CSV, docs to Word, Markdown or PDF. Everything runs on your machine, with no account and no upload. Credit @dotey

tweets.text:
Axios 称 Anthropic 内部认为该把部分决策权交给超级智能，Dario 发长文否认：把治理交给 AI 是“糟糕的主意”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei 11 月 25 日在 X 上发长文，否认自己主张“把人类自由意志交给 AI”，说这种说法“荒谬”。他回应的是 Axios 当天早上的独家报道，标题是“竞争对手 AI 领袖反对 Anthropic 把人类主导权交给 AI 的愿景”。

【Axios 报道了什么】

Axios 援引不具名的知情人说，Anthropic 内部有一种常见看法：AI 迟早强大到人类应该把一部分决策权交给超级智能，而且很多时候这样做是对的。批评者认为，这会一步步滑向放弃自由意志。

Axios 拿 Dario 过去的话做佐证。2024 年的长文《慈爱的机器》（Machines of Loving Grace）设想过一种经济，由 AI 按“AI 系统认为值得奖励人类的东西”给人分配资源。2026 年 2 月接受 CBS 采访时，Dario 说对手可能先用上全自主武器，所以这种武器“有一天可能是保卫民主所需要的”。Axios 还提到一张在诉讼中曝光的旧幻灯片，把 Anthropic 的愿景写成“由盒子里的神统治的乌托邦”。

报道里的“对手”有三位。OpenAI CEO Sam Altman 11 月 4 日发推说“人永远应该掌控未来”，并反对让人沦为去做“AI 系统认为值得奖励人类的事”，引号里这句和《慈爱的机器》原文一字不差。Meta 首席 AI 官 Alexandr Wang 11 月 22 日发文说，不应该接受把社会“移交”给 AI。OpenAI 的 Dean Ball 在 OpenAI 官网发文，把这种看法叫作“沉默的共识”：人类把公司和政府交给机器，自己像坐在豪车后座、管不了方向的乘客。Axios 说，这几位都没有点名 Anthropic。

Anthropic 发言人对 Axios 说，Dario 在很多公开场合都主张人类掌控 AI，公司也训练 Claude 不去破坏人类监督。

【Dario 的回应】

Dario 把问题拆成两件事。

第一件是谁来治理社会。Dario 说，AI 必须由合法的民主程序来管，把治理交给 AI 是“糟糕的主意”。他拿专制作类比：几千年来，主张专制的人都说专制决策更快、更果断，就算真是这样，也不该为了效率或安全牺牲合法性和自决权，这套道理同样适用于 AI。

Dario 列了自己的文章和访谈作证。《慈爱的机器》有一节讲用 AI 帮公民凝聚共识、找到妥协；今年 1 月的《技术的青春期》有一整节讲反对 AI 驱动的暴政，还警告 AI 公司自己夺权；9 月接受 CBS 采访时，Dario 说愿意让几个民主选举的政府对 AI 进行某种联合监督。

第二件是具体任务交给 AI 做到什么程度，比如开车、设计抗癌药、从头到尾写软件。Dario 说这方面他的看法有好有坏：很多时候值得做，能救很多命，但有四处要设限。

一是让 AI 自己造下一代 AI，也就是“递归自我改进”，进步可能快到人类管不住。二是端到端自动化可能造成严重失业，有些部署应该放慢甚至暂停。三是用 AI 做安全对齐研究要小心，因为不一定能信任 AI 交出的成果。四是有些事人就是想自己做，哪怕 AI 做得更好。

第一条 Dario 引用的是 Anthropic 11 月 2 日更新的上市招股书。招股书写道，公司预计无法安全地让 Claude 在没有人类有效监督和理解的情况下，完全自主地设计和构建下一代前沿模型。同一份文件也写了，按内部估计，未来的模型可能“很快”达到公司安全政策里“AI 带来大幅加速”的门槛。

【“别家和我没区别”】

Dario 说，在哪些任务该自动化这件事上，其他 AI 公司和他看法差不多：各家都在发布越来越能自动干活的模型，也都说自己懂风险、有防护。

Dario 说，拿自主武器那句话说他和别家不同“相当荒谬”。今年 2 月，Anthropic 拒绝五角大楼取消“不用于全自主武器、不用于大规模监控美国人”这两条限制，被国防部长 Hegseth 列为供应链风险。Dario 说他冒着公司前途和法律制裁的风险坚持了下来，“没有别的 AI 公司这么做”。

Dario 最后说，一些 AI CEO 在做“凭感觉的商业和政治定位”，反复喊“人类掌控与能动性”“AI 只该是工具”这类口号，产品上却没有任何不同，也没认真想过口号背后的难题。Dario 没点名，Axios 报道里喊这类口号的正是 Altman 和 Wang。

Axios 关于 Anthropic 内部看法的说法全部来自不具名人士，Dario 的长文只谈他本人的立场，没有回应这一点。“没有别的公司拒绝自主武器”是 Dario 自己的说法。

No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.
